platforms.title: Your Post-Lunch Slump Might Not Be a Food Coma
platforms.meta_description: That drowsiness after lunch might not be a food coma — it can be reactive hypoglycemia after a blood sugar spike, according to Mayo Clinic and walking studies.
platforms.body_html:
Some afternoons, staying awake at your desk after lunch feels almost impossible. Most people write it off as a "food coma," but the drowsiness can actually be a reactive hypoglycemia response — your blood sugar spiking and then crashing below where it started. How fast a meal gets absorbed matters more than how much you ate.

Sugar Rush vs. What's Actually Happening in Your Body

Meals high in refined carbohydrates and sugar push blood glucose up quickly. The pancreas responds by releasing a large, fast burst of insulin to bring it back down — and when that burst overshoots, blood sugar drops below where it started, a pattern Mayo Clinic describes as reactive hypoglycemia, typically showing up one to four hours after eating. The brain runs almost entirely on glucose, so it's hit first when levels fall, and the same insulin surge also raises tryptophan and serotonin in the brain, which deepens the drowsiness on top of the glucose dip.

Reactive Hypoglycemia vs. Just Needing More Sleep — How to Tell the Difference

First, try changing the order you eat things in. Eating vegetables and protein before carbohydrates slows how fast the meal's sugar reaches your bloodstream, even if the plate itself doesn't change.

Second, walk after you eat. A study published in the American Diabetes Association's journal Diabetes Care found that three 15-minute walks after meals meaningfully improved glucose control over a full day, and a more recent trial found that a 10-minute walk immediately after eating was especially effective at blunting the peak of the blood sugar spike. You don't need a workout — just standing up and moving lets your muscles pull glucose out of the bloodstream instead of leaving it to insulin alone.

Third, it helps to notice which of your regular meals hit hardest. Sweetened coffee drinks, white bagels, glazed pastries, and meat glazed in sugary sauce tend to be absorbed fast because there's little fiber or protein slowing things down. You don't have to cut these out entirely — but reordering your plate and taking a short walk afterward can meaningfully cut down the wall of drowsiness that follows.

It also helps to actually track this instead of guessing. For a week, jot down what you ate for lunch and how you felt roughly 60 to 90 minutes later — foggy and heavy-eyed, or just normally full. A pattern usually shows up fast: the days built around a sweetened drink or a bread-heavy plate tend to cluster together, while days with more vegetables and protein rarely do. That short log turns a vague daily struggle into something you can actually plan around instead of just pushing through.

Checklist to remember: what you ate, in what order, how fast it went down, and whether you moved afterward — those four factors explain most afternoon crashes better than "I just need more sleep" does. If the slump is severe, involves shakiness or sweating, or happens after nearly every meal, it's worth mentioning to a doctor rather than working around it indefinitely.
